title: Isotope niches differ ontogenetically among key rocky reef predators
content:
Abstract

Predator niche partitioning occurs based on access to prey and feeding ability, which can change spatially and temporally, potentially becoming specialized with predator size. Isotopic niche analysis infers differences in dietary composition or niche, elucidating ecological links between sympatric predators and size effects. However, comparisons among temperate reef predators are scarce. In southeast (SE) Australia, New South Wales, the sympatric Palinurid Sagmariasus verreauxi (Eastern Rock Lobster), Sparid Chrysophyrus auratus (Snapper), and Wrasse Achoerodus viridis (Eastern Blue Groper) are considered large, key predators that structure benthic reef communities, yet their relative isotopic and trophic niches are unknown. To investigate, we used δ13C and δ15N muscle values from these species from seven regions > 1250 km of SE Australian coastline. Bayesian isotopic niche analysis showed varied regional niche size and overlap within species for Lobster (0.74–3.27‰2, 5.87–51.03%) and Snapper (0.87–3.30‰2, 10.57–68.45%) but not Blue Groper (1.36–1.50 ‰2, 17.67–23.74%), suggesting diets differ spatially. At large body sizes, niches were ~ 50% smaller for Lobster and Blue Groper but ~ 15% larger for Snapper, suggesting diets differ ontogenetically. Between species, Lobster niche was ~ 30% larger than fishes suggesting lobsters have more varied diets. Our results indicate that Lobster and Blue Groper follow general predator models using more specific resources with size, while Snapper may not. Overall, we found low niche overlap between these species indicating different overall niches despite Lobster, Snapper, and Blue Groper being sympatric rocky reef predators.
